items.prose: A chart's log price axis draws the rise from £50 to £100 as 1 cm.
items.question: What height does it give the rise from £100 to £800?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count doublings from £100 to £800.

byKey.linear: You scaled by pounds: £700 is 14 times £50. On a log axis only ratios count.
byKey.ratio: A ratio of 8 is three doublings, not eight.

explain.text: £100 → £200 → £400 → £800 is three doublings. Each doubling has the same height on a log axis, 1 cm here, so the move is 3 cm.

items.prose: Each series below is switched to `ax.set_yscale("log")`.
items.question: Which chart loses values without any warning?

options.text: A strategy's cumulative P&L, starting at £0.00

options.why: Every value is positive, so all of it fits on a log axis.
A positive price fits on a log axis; this is where log axes help most.
An equity curve above zero loses nothing.

feedback.correct: The zero and any losses below it vanish.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a series that reaches zero.

explain.text: A log axis has no place for zero or negatives. matplotlib clips them off the chart without a warning, so the P&L chart loses its start and every losing stretch below zero.

options.why: There are only two rows. The first index, 1, is the row.
Columns count from 0, so 2 is the third column, the right-hand one.
Row 1 is the second row, the bottom one here.

feedback.correct: Row 1 of 0 to 1, column 2 of 0 to 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Row first, column second, both from 0.

explain.text: `plt.subplots(2, 3)` makes rows 0 to 1 and columns 0 to 2. `axes[1, 2]` is the last of each: the bottom right.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The height in inches is the second number of `figsize`.

byKey.default: That uses the default 100 dpi; this save asks for 150.

explain.text: The figure is 6 inches tall, and 150 dpi makes that 900 pixels. With `bbox_inches="tight"` the file would be slightly smaller.

items.prose: A chart has two y axes: ACME on the left and BETA on the right. The two lines cross in June. A colleague writes “BETA overtook ACME in June”.
items.question: What is wrong with that sentence?

options.text: The crossing comes from the chosen axis ranges
Charts lag, so BETA overtook ACME in May
options.why: No lag is involved. The crossing could be moved to any month by changing BETA's axis.

options.text: Nothing, if both axes are labelled
options.why: Labels do not fix it. The ranges themselves decide where the lines meet.

options.text: It is only true on a log axis
options.why: A log axis would move the crossing again. The problem is the second axis.

feedback.correct: With two axes, crossings are set by choice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would happen to the crossing if BETA's axis changed.

explain.text: Stretch or slide BETA's axis and the crossing moves to another month. To compare the two, rebase both to 100 on one axis.

items.question: Where does its line end when rebased to 100?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale 100 by last over first.

byKey.diff: You added the £8 rise to 100. Rebasing uses the ratio, a 12.5% rise.
byKey.ratio: That is the ratio. Multiply by 100.

explain.text: £72 is 1.125 times £64, so the rebased line ends at 112.5: a 12.5% rise, comparable with any other rebased line.

items.prose: A bar chart's y axis starts at £90. Last year's bar is £100.00 and this year's is £96.00, a fall of 4%.
items.question: What fall do the drawn bars suggest, in %?

feedback.correct: Lengths 10 and 6 look like a 40% fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each bar from £90.

byKey.true: That is the real fall. The drawn bars start at £90, so they are 10 and 6 long.
byKey.share: That is the share left, 6 / 10. The fall is that minus 1.

explain.text: From £90 the bars are 10 and 6 long, so the eye reads $6/10 - 1 = -40\%$, ten times the true 4%. Bars start at zero.

items.prose: A fund lost 20% over two years, then gained 30% over the next twelve months. Its factsheet charts only those twelve months.
items.question: What is the honest fix?

options.text: Chart the whole history, or a standard period, so the reader sees the fall too
Use a log axis for the twelve months
options.why: An axis cannot restore the two years the window leaves out.

options.text: Start the y axis at zero
options.why: Zero matters for bars. The problem here is the window, not the axis.
A precise label on a cherry-picked window still flatters.

feedback.correct: Show the period the reader needs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The problem is which months are shown.

explain.text: Over three years the fund is at $0.80 \times 1.30 = 1.04$, up 4%. A window starting at the low turns that into +30%. Show the whole history, or say why the window starts where it does.

items.question: What is the maximum drawdown, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the running peak and the worst fall below it.

byKey.range: You used the lowest and highest closes. The £30.00 low came first, so it was never a fall.
byKey.second: That is the second fall, £50.00 to £42.50. The first, from £45.00, was deeper.

explain.text: The running peak is £45.00 when the price drops to £36.00: −20%. The later dip from £50.00 to £42.50 is only −15%.

items.prose: Over the past year a stock's daily returns had a sample standard deviation of 1.10%.
items.question: Scaled to a year of 252 trading days, what is that volatility, in %?

byKey.times: You multiplied by 252. Standard deviation scales with the square root of time.
byKey.months: That uses √12, for monthly data. These are daily returns.

explain.text: Variances add over independent days, so a year's standard deviation is $\sqrt{252} \approx 15.87$ daily ones: $1.10\% \times 15.87 = 17.46\%$.
